issues.legal_issue: A bill pending before a State Legislature does not lapse merely because the House is prorogued before the Constitution commences.
material_facts: The Bill had been introduced and was pending before the State Legislature when the House was prorogued.
The Bill was later reintroduced and enacted.
issues.conclusion: The Bill remained pending despite prorogation and therefore was pending when the Constitution commenced.
issues.legal_principle: Section 73 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and article 196 of the Constitution provide that a pending Bill does not lapse by reason of prorogation of the House or Houses. The Court rejected the argument that prorogation caused this Bill to lapse.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_acquis: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law enacted by a State Legislature to acquire property.
predicates.state_legislative_bill_pending: The Bill that became the challenged law was pending before the State Legislature.
predicates.house_prorogued_before_constitution_comm: The House was prorogued before the Constitution commenced.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a State acquisition law whose Bill was pending when the House was prorogued before the Constitution commenced, the Bill remains pending despite prorogation.

issues.legal_issue: A State law acquiring an estate that was pending when the Constitution commenced and received presidential assent is protected from a challenge based on Part III rights.
material_facts: The Bill was pending before the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
The enacted law received the President's assent.
The law provided for acquisition of estates.
issues.conclusion: The Act could not be invalidated on the basis of rights in Part III of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(4) applied because the Bill was pending when the Constitution commenced. Article 31A, subject to its assent requirement for State laws, and article 31B also protected the law from attack based on Part III. The Court held that Part III was not repealed, but that the relevant protections prevented the appellants from challenging this law on those grounds.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_estate: A party challenges a State law that provides for acquisition of estates.
predicates.bill_pending_at_constitution_commencemen: The Bill that became the law was pending before the Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
predicates.presidential_assent_received: The State law received the President's assent.

issues.definition: A State estate-acquisition law is protected from a Part III challenge when its Bill was pending at the commencement of the Constitution and the law received presidential assent.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation scheme for acquisition of an entire estate is not illusory merely because it values compensation by reference to net income and provides no separate payment for non-income-producing components.
material_facts: The law acquired estates as a whole, including income-producing and non-income-producing property.
It calculated compensation by reference to the estate's net assets and made compensation payable to each intermediary.
Compensation became due upon vesting, and the amount was determined by an assessment officer subject to appeal.
The law allowed payment in cash, bonds, or a combination, with the method to be prescribed by the Government.
issues.conclusion: The compensation provisions were not illusory or invalid merely because they did not provide an equivalent market value or separately compensate non-income-producing property; compensation was legally due. Rules prescribing an unreasonably remote time for payment could separately be challenged as an abuse of power.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied article 31(2) and the legislative entries concerning acquisition and compensation, while holding that article 31(4) answered challenges to the adequacy of compensation in these appeals. It distinguished acquisition of an entire estate, valued on net income, from acquisition of separate pieces of property. The statutory provisions made payment obligatory, and the compensation amount was determined by an officer with an appeal available.

rule.if: challenge_to_compensation_for_estate_acquisition and entire_estate_acquired and compensation_legally_due and compensation_amount_assessed_with_appeal

predicates.challenge_to_compensation_for_estate_acq: A party challenges the compensation provided for acquisition of an estate.
predicates.entire_estate_acquired: The acquisition covers the estate as a whole rather than separate, selected pieces of property.
predicates.compensation_legally_due: The law makes payment of compensation obligatory upon acquisition.
predicates.compensation_amount_assessed_with_appeal: An official determines the compensation amount and the affected person can appeal that determination.

issues.definition: When an entire estate is acquired and compensation is legally due in an amount determined through an appealable assessment, the scheme is not illusory merely because it does not separately pay market value for each component.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of estates to reform land tenure, raise the status of cultivators, and manage land for the community is for a public purpose even when private individuals receive tenure rights after acquisition.
material_facts: The law vested estates in the State and provided for land to vest in village bodies for management under State supervision.
It created or enlarged cultivators' tenure rights and provided for agrarian reforms, including cooperative farming and village self-government.
The acquired property was not taken for the private benefit of a particular individual, and the reform applied to people already in possession of land.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition had a public purpose and was not invalid for want of one.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of public purpose is elastic and depends on the statute, the time, and society's needs; the inquiry is whether the acquisition serves the general interest of the community rather than an individual's private interest. The Court considered the constitutional objectives and the Act as a whole, and distinguished redistribution for community-wide agrarian reform from taking one person's property solely for another's private use. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition_for_: A party challenges compulsory acquisition undertaken as part of land-tenure reform.
predicates.acquisition_serves_community_wide_tenure: The acquisition enables reforms intended to change tenure arrangements and benefit the community generally.
predicates.property_not_transferred_for_private_ben: The acquired property is not taken to give it for the private benefit of a particular person.

issues.definition: Compulsory acquisition for land reform serves a public purpose when it advances community-wide tenure reform rather than a particular person's private benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may delegate rulemaking about implementation details when the statute itself establishes the main legislative principles.
material_facts: The Act established the main principles governing acquisition and compensation.
It left details such as interest rates and the form, proportion, and timing of compensation payments to executive rules.
issues.conclusion: The delegation was within permissible limits and did not delegate essential legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature may set the main principles and leave matters of detail to rulemaking. The Court considered sections 6(e), 6(g), and 68 of the Act and held that the matters left to the Government were details rather than essential legislative choices. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_rulemaking: A party challenges authority delegated by a statute to the executive to make rules.
predicates.statute_sets_main_legislative_principles: The statute itself establishes the principal policy and governing standards.
predicates.delegated_matters_are_implementation_det: The delegated matters concern details for implementing the statutory scheme.

issues.definition: Delegation is permissible when the statute establishes the main principles and leaves only implementation details to executive rulemaking.

issues.legal_issue: A legislative body with authority over property may legislate to alter or acquire rights granted by the Crown unless the governing constitutional instrument expressly prohibits it.
material_facts: The appellants relied on land grants and asserted that the legislature could not alter the rights created by those grants.
The acquisition law concerned property within the legislative authority of the State Legislature.
issues.conclusion: The land grants did not prevent the legislature from legislating about the property, and the taluqdari lands were not immune from acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: A Crown grant does not, by itself, prevent a legislature from legislating within its competence to alter or acquire the granted rights. The Court relied on Thakur Jagannath Baksh Singh v. United Provinces, [1946] F.C.R. 111, which held that a Crown grant does not bar subsequent legislation absent an express prohibition.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_of_granted_land: A party challenges a law that acquires land or rights previously granted by the Crown.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_property: The legislature enacting the law has authority over the subject matter of the property.
predicates.no_express_constitutional_bar_to_legisla: The governing constitutional instrument contains no express prohibition against legislation affecting the grant.

issues.definition: A Crown grant does not prevent acquisition legislation when the legislature has authority over the property and no express constitutional bar applies.

issues.legal_issue: A private covenant guaranteeing ownership and enjoyment of property does not prevent a competent legislature from acquiring that property under a later law, and a dispute arising from the covenant may fall outside the Court's jurisdiction.
material_facts: A covenant identified certain property as the ruler's private property and guaranteed its ownership, use, and enjoyment.
The acquisition law treated the property as private property and provided compensation for its acquisition.
The Government denied that the privy purse had been fixed in reliance on income from the property, and no material was produced to displace that denial.
The Government of India signed the covenant as a guarantor and concurring party.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not breach the guarantee; the claim based on the alleged privy-purse arrangement was unsupported, and article 363 barred the Court from deciding the covenant dispute.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that article 362 did not invalidate the acquisition in these circumstances: the property was treated as private property and acquired on that basis, while article 362 imposed no enforceable legal obligation on the legislature. It further held that article 363 applied to a dispute arising out of the covenant because the Government of India was a party to it. The Court relied on its earlier treatment of a similar issue in the Madhya Pradesh petitions.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_of_covenant_gua: A party challenges acquisition of property said to be protected by a covenant with a ruler.
predicates.property_treated_as_private_and_compensa: The acquisition law recognizes the property as private property and provides compensation for its acquisition.
predicates.government_was_party_to_covenant: The government was a party to or guarantor of the covenant relied upon.

issues.definition: When the acquired property is treated as private and compensated, and the government was a party to the covenant, the covenant does not invalidate the acquisition and a dispute arising from it is barred.

issues.legal_issue: Property dedicated to religious or charitable purposes is not immune from compulsory acquisition for a public purpose.
material_facts: Religious institutions held endowed properties and used income from those properties for religious and charitable activities.
The acquisition law provided compensation based on the institutions' net income from the properties.
issues.conclusion: The properties could be acquired, and their prior dedication to religious or charitable purposes did not make them immune from acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: A private dedication of property to charity does not exempt it from the sovereign power of compulsory acquisition for public purposes. The Court also held that compensation based on the net income meant that the acquisition did not, on the facts advanced, adversely affect the charity. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition_of_e: A party challenges compulsory acquisition of property held by a religious or charitable institution.
predicates.property_dedicated_to_charitable_or_reli: The property has been dedicated to religious or charitable purposes.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_public_purpose: The acquisition serves a public purpose.

issues.definition: Property dedicated to religious or charitable use is not immune from compulsory acquisition when the acquisition serves a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition notification authorized by a valid statute is not invalid merely because the notification itself is not independently protected from a fundamental-rights challenge.
material_facts: The Act authorized the State Government to issue a notification bringing estates within the acquisition scheme.
The challenge to the notification rested on the contention that it was not protected by provisions that sheltered the Act.
issues.conclusion: The notification could not be held invalid on that ground because it was consequential to a valid statute.
issues.legal_principle: A notification that is consequential to a valid statute does not become invalid merely because it is an executive act; the Court rejected the challenge as dependent on an erroneous separation of the notification from the statute that authorized it. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_notification_under_acquisit: A party challenges an executive notification issued under an acquisition statute.
predicates.statute_is_valid: The statute authorizing the notification is valid.
predicates.notification_is_consequential_to_statute: The notification implements or follows from the statute's authorization.

issues.definition: A consequential notification under a valid acquisition statute is not invalid merely because the notification is executive in form.

issues.legal_issue: A lawfully enacted acquisition statute is not invalid merely because affected owners previously had rights or remedies under general land-acquisition legislation.
material_facts: The appellants asserted that existing rights under general land-acquisition legislation could not be displaced by the challenged statute.
The challenged statute established a separate scheme for acquiring estates.
issues.conclusion: The asserted pre-existing rights under general land-acquisition legislation did not invalidate the challenged statute.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the contention, applying the reasons it had given in the Bihar appeals. The supplied judgment does not set out those reasons in detail.

predicates.challenge_to_specific_acquisition_statut: A party challenges a statute that establishes a specific scheme for compulsory acquisition.
predicates.prior_general_acquisition_remedy_asserte: The party relies on rights or remedies under pre-existing general acquisition legislation.
predicates.statute_enacted_within_legislative_compe: The statute was enacted within the legislature's authority.

issues.definition: A party's reliance on a prior general acquisition remedy does not invalidate a specific acquisition statute enacted within legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A statute may acquire less than the entirety of an owner's interests in land when the legislature considers the lesser interest sufficient for the public purpose.
material_facts: The appellants argued that rights in land could not be acquired separately from the land or that proprietary rights could not be acquired while other rights remained with the owners.
The Act acquired intermediary rights while leaving or creating other tenure rights under its scheme.
issues.conclusion: The legislature could acquire part of an owner's rights without acquiring the entirety of the owner's interest.
issues.legal_principle: The Government may acquire the whole of an owner's rights or only a part, if the part is what is needed for public purposes; leasehold and other limited interests may also be acquired. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_partial_acquisition_of_land: A party challenges acquisition of only some rights or interests associated with land.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_to_acquire_pro: The legislature has authority to provide for acquisition of property.
predicates.acquired_interest_is_sufficient_for_publ: The interest acquired is the interest needed to serve the public purpose.

issues.definition: A legislature may acquire only the land interest needed for a public purpose when it has authority to provide for acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A law providing for acquisition of estates under the legislative power over acquisition is not invalid merely because it also affects the right to hold property.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the law should be treated as legislation concerning land and land tenures and that it unreasonably restricted the right to hold property.
The Act provided for compulsory acquisition of estates and had the protections identified by the Court against challenges based on Part III.
issues.conclusion: The Act was enacted under the legislative power relating to acquisition, not the power concerning land and land tenures, and the challenge under the right to hold property failed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the law fell under entry 36 of List II, concerning acquisition, rather than entry 18 of List II, concerning land and land tenures. It further held that the protections in articles 31(4), 31A, and 31B prevented reliance on Part III to invalidate the law.

predicates.challenge_to_estate_acquisition_law: A party challenges a law providing for acquisition of estates.
predicates.law_principally_provides_for_compulsory_: The law's principal subject is compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.law_is_protected_from_part_three_challen: The law is protected from invalidation based on rights in Part III.

issues.definition: A property-right challenge does not invalidate an estate-acquisition law whose principal subject is compulsory acquisition and which is protected from a Part III challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A law is not a fraud on the Constitution merely because earlier legislation is alleged to have reduced the value or income of property later acquired.
material_facts: The appellants pointed to several earlier enactments and alleged that they formed a scheme to deprive landowners of compensation.
The cited enactments predated the Constitution and were not shown to be connected with acquisition under the challenged Act.
issues.conclusion: The fraud-on-the-Constitution contention failed because the earlier enactments had no demonstrated connection with the acquisition law.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the allegation as founded on a confusion of thought: the earlier enactments were enacted before the Constitution and were not shown to have any connection with acquisition of the properties under the challenged statute. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_law_as_constitu: A party alleges that an acquisition law is a fraud on the Constitution.
predicates.alleged_prior_measures_predate_constitut: The earlier measures relied on by the party were enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.no_connection_shown_between_prior_measur: The party does not show that the earlier measures were connected with the acquisition under the challenged law.

issues.definition: An allegation of constitutional fraud fails when the earlier measures predate the Constitution and are not shown to be connected with the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A statute governing the management of religious endowments does not bar acquisition of the property it concerns unless it applies to the property and prohibits acquisition.
material_facts: An appellant argued that a statute concerning religious endowments prevented acquisition of endowed land.
The record did not establish that the management statute applied to the properties, and the statute dealt with management rather than acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The religious-endowments legislation did not prevent acquisition of the properties.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the cited statute concerned management of certain properties and did not stand in the way of their acquisition; its application to the properties in question had not been proved. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_of_endowment_pr: A party challenges acquisition of property associated with a religious endowment.
predicates.management_law_applies_only_to_managemen: The cited law governs management of property rather than its acquisition.
predicates.no_acquisition_bar_established: The party does not establish that the law prohibits acquisition of the property.

issues.definition: A law concerned with management does not prevent acquisition when no prohibition on acquisition is established.
